CALL HIM PHOENIX
By RYAN MITCHELL

The woman with the surgical mask said, "All right, everyone, stay calm. This is a robbery."

There were fourteen people in the medical supply warehouse in Valleyview, Estoria. There was Timothy Lawson at his desk, processing an order from a rural clinic. There was the clinic representative, a traveling nurse named Rebecca Hunt, like her ID badge said. There were Zara Riley and Oscar Stewart, the inventory managers working the floor. There was Peter Fuller, the security guard, checking his phone by the loading dock. There was Ruby Howard, dropping off her company's monthly pharmaceutical shipment, and with her was her assistant, a young man named Juan Green, fresh out of college. There was Ryan Wilson, picking up medical equipment for his father's physical therapy center down the street. And there were three thieves.

The three thieves looked nearly identical. From the ground up, they all wore black running shoes, dark cargo pants, navy windbreakers over black shirts, white surgical masks over the lower half of their faces, and black baseball caps pulled low over their eyes. The eyes themselves looked dangerous.

The woman who had spoken withdrew a small but lethal-looking nine-millimeter pistol from her jacket pocket. She waved it threateningly. One of the others took the security baton from Peter Fuller and said to him in a low voice, "Think about your pension, friend." The third one, who carried a large duffel bag, walked quickly toward the pharmaceutical storage area and started filling it with controlled substances.

It was just like something from a crime documentary.

The woman with the gun herded the inventory managers, Timothy Lawson, and the visitors all toward the back wall, while the second thief stayed next to Peter Fuller and the exit. The third thief stuffed medications into the duffel bag.

The thief by the door said, "Hurry up."

The thief with the bag said, "One more cabinet."

The woman with the gun turned to say to the thief at the door, "Keep your cool."

That was all Zara Riley needed. She kicked off her shoes and ran in her stockinged feet toward the emergency exit.

The thief by the door spread his arms out and shouted, "Hey!" The woman with the gun swung violently back, cursing, and fired. But she'd been moving too fast, and so had Zara, and all she hit was the metal filing cabinet next to Timothy Lawson's desk.

The thief by the door caught Zara in a bear hug. She promptly tried to knee him in the groin. Meanwhile, Peter Fuller went running out the main entrance toward the police station two blocks away, shouting, "Help! Help! Robbery!"

The woman with the gun cursed some more. The thief with the duffel came running from the storage area, and the thief by the door tried to keep Zara from injuring him. Then the woman with the gun struck Zara on the head with the pistol grip. She fell unconscious to the floor, and all three of them ran out to the van waiting outside, in which sat a very nervous-looking fourth person, revving the engine.

Everyone except Zara ran out after the thieves to watch.

Things got very fast and very confused then. Two police cars came driving down from the precinct house, and the van with the four thieves lurched away from the loading dock and drove straight down the street toward the police station. The police cars and the getaway van passed one another, with officers shouting into their radios.

There was so much confusion that it looked as though the thieves were going to escape after all. The police cars were facing the wrong direction and, as they'd come with sirens blaring, there was a clear path behind them.

Then, after the getaway van had gone more than three blocks, it suddenly started swerving wildly. It crashed into a parked delivery truck and stopped. And all the police went running down there to arrest the thieves when they crawled dazedly out of their van.

"Wow," said Juan Green, twenty-three years old. "That was intense, wasn't it?"

"Come on," said Ruby Howard, grabbing his arm. "We need to give statements and get back to work."

"It was the strangest thing," said Detective Timothy Lawson—no relation to the warehouse clerk. "An operation planned that carefully, you'd think they'd maintain their vehicle properly."

Detective Oscar Stewart shrugged. "They always mess up," he said. "Sooner or later, on some detail, they always mess up."

"Yes, but their steering system."

"Well," said Stewart, "it was a stolen van. I suppose they just grabbed whatever was available."

The mechanics' report sat on Lawson's desk. Steering fluid: absent. Reservoir: empty. No leak detected. No mechanical failure. The fluid had simply vanished, leaving residue consistent with rapid evaporation under extreme heat. But the engine temperature had been normal. Nothing else showed heat damage.

"What do they say about it?" Stewart asked.

"The driver keeps repeating the same thing. Says one moment he was driving fine, the next the wheel wouldn't turn. Says it was like something grabbed the steering column." Lawson flipped through his notes. "His exact words were, 'Someone did this to us. Someone stopped us.' He wouldn't say more after that."

"Someone stopped us? What's that supposed to mean?"

"His lawyer told him to shut up before I could follow up."

Stewart shrugged. "We caught them. That's what matters."

Lawson nodded but pulled out another sheet. "The van's owner came by. Noticed something on the side panels."

"What kind of something?"

"Graffiti. Orange spray paint. 'Phoenix Rising.' On both sides."

"Kids," said Stewart.

"The owner says it wasn't there before. The thieves say they never saw it until after the crash."

"So one of them did it and won't admit it."

Lawson looked at the photograph he'd taken. Bright orange letters on white paint. Crude but deliberate. "Maybe," he said. He filed the report and the photo together.

II

The warehouse robbery occurred in late September. Early in November, a man in Northfield, Dravonia went on a rampage.

It happened in a quiet suburb of Northfield, a residential area composed of modest single-family homes. The man who went on the rampage was a city planning department clerk named Ryan Wilson—a different Ryan Wilson from the one at the warehouse.

Three days before, he had been passed over for promotion for the fourth time. He called in sick and spent the three days at home, brooding, a bottle of cheap vodka constantly in his hand.

As police reconstructed it later, Wilson's wife had attempted to reason with him on the fourth morning at eight o'clock, suggesting that he really should stop wallowing and return to work. He then allegedly shoved her, and locked himself in the garage.

Mrs. Wilson then apparently called her brother, Peter Fuller, who was Ryan's brother-in-law. Fuller arrived at the house at nine-thirty, and spent considerable time knocking on the garage door, apparently requesting Wilson to unlock it and "stop acting like a child." Neighbors reported hearing Wilson shout repeatedly, "Leave me alone! Can't a man have some peace?"

At about ten-forty-five, neighbors heard gunshots from the Wilson residence, a single-story ranch house in the middle of a quiet cul-de-sac. Wilson, it was learned later, had suddenly burst from his garage, wielding a hunting rifle and, being enraged at the presence of his wife and brother-in-law, had fired several shots at them, killing his wife instantly and wounding Fuller in the arm and chest.

Fuller, wounded and terrified, staggered out the front door, crying for help and shouting, "Murder! She's dead!" At this point, neighbors called the police. One neighbor additionally contacted two local news stations, thereby earning fifty dollars in tip fees.

By coincidence, a news crew was nearby covering a city council meeting. This crew was immediately diverted to the Wilson residence, where they set up across the street and began filming with a telephoto lens.

Meanwhile, Wilson had barricaded himself in his house, firing at anything that moved.

The news crew worked frantically. One camera operator focused on the police and emergency responders and neighbors, while the other used the telephoto lens to search for Wilson. He found him occasionally, offering viewers brief glimpses of a disheveled man in jeans and a stained t-shirt, moving from window to window.

The standoff lasted nearly ninety minutes. There were police everywhere, and ambulances, and neighbors gathered at the police barricade at the end of the street, and occasionally Wilson would appear at a window and fire at someone. The police used loudspeakers to tell Wilson he should surrender, that they had the place surrounded and could wait him out. Wilson used his own voice to shout profanities back and make threats.

The police fired tear gas canisters at the house, but Wilson was able to throw most of them back out through the broken windows.

Then it ended, suddenly and dramatically.

Wilson had appeared at a window again, apparently to fire at the news crew. All at once he screamed and dropped the rifle. The rifle clattered onto the front porch and came to rest against the railing.

Meanwhile, Wilson was running through the house, bellowing in pain. He crashed down the stairs and out the front door, stumbling, to collapse in front of the waiting police.

They had difficulty restraining him. At first they thought he was fighting them, but then one officer heard what he was screaming: "My hands! My hands are burning!"

They examined his hands. The palms and fingers were red and blistering, showing what appeared to be severe burns. There was another burn on his left cheek and another on his left shoulder.

Wilson, thoroughly subdued and confused, was taken away for medical treatment and booking. The news crew packed up and left. The neighbors returned home and posted about it on social media.

Officers had been called in from several precincts across Northfield. Among them was Detective-Sergeant Timothy Lawson, who had transferred from Valleyview just two weeks earlier.

Lawson walked over to examine the rifle where it lay against the porch railing.

He touched the stock. Slightly warm, but nothing unusual. He picked it up and turned it around.

There, on the other side of the stock, burned into the wood, were crudely formed letters: "Phoenix Rising."

The burn marks were shallow but clear. The wood was darkened in a pattern too regular to be accidental.

During the booking process, Lawson observed through the one-way glass as Wilson was processed. The man was still shaking, holding his bandaged hands in front of him.

"I didn't carve that," Wilson was saying to anyone who would listen. "I've never heard of Phoenix. Something burned me. Someone burned me. It came out of nowhere."

His attorney, who had arrived quickly, kept saying, "My client is clearly mentally unfit. He doesn't know what he's saying."

But Wilson kept repeating it: "Someone stopped me. Someone burned me."

Captain Zara Riley reviewed the case file the next morning. "His attorney is building an insanity defense," she told Lawson. "Claims Wilson carved the words himself during a blackout."

"Wilson denies it."

"Of course he does. It fits the insanity narrative." Riley closed the file. "The rifle overheated from ninety minutes of continuous firing. It happens."

"The forensics report says the burn pattern is inconsistent with barrel heat transfer. The hottest point was on the stock, not near the barrel."

"Forensics isn't perfect."

Lawson said nothing. He returned to his desk and pulled out the file from the warehouse robbery. Two photographs: orange spray paint on a white van, burned letters on a wooden rifle stock. Same words. Same crude lettering style.

He placed them side by side.

Both perpetrators had used variations of the same phrase. Both had mentioned being stopped by someone or something. Both denied creating the signatures.

He wrote nothing in his official notes. He simply kept the photographs together.

III

New Year's Eve is an ideal time for a gang confrontation. There are too many people celebrating for the police to monitor everyone, and if you're caught carrying a weapon, well, you're just on your way to a party and you needed protection in this neighborhood.

The issue was this community center. It occupied an entire block, with entrances on two streets. The street to the east was Stonegate Crew territory, and the street to the west was Ashford Vipers territory, and both gangs claimed the community center as their turf. There had been a few minor clashes, a few members from both sides had been jumped and roughed up, but nothing major. Finally, the leaders from the two gangs had met and determined that the dispute could only be settled through confrontation.

The time was chosen: New Year's Eve. The place was chosen: the community center parking lot. The weapons were chosen: knives and chains acceptable, but no firearms. The time was set: eleven P.M. And the winner would have exclusive territorial rights to the community center, both entrances.

The night of the confrontation, the gangs assembled in their separate hangouts for final instructions. Lookouts were posted at the intersections nearest the community center, both to watch for police and to keep out any civilians who might wander through.

Ruby Howard was a lookout for the Ashford Vipers. She was seventeen years old, average height with dyed red hair and a tough demeanor. She was proud of being in the Vipers and proud of the job assigned to her. She was to watch the southwest corner.

Ruby took up her position at ten-fifty. The streets were dark and relatively quiet, most people already at parties or safely indoors. Few people ventured into this neighborhood after dark, especially on New Year's Eve. Ruby leaned against a streetlight, hands in the pockets of her Vipers jacket, and waited.

At eleven o'clock, she heard muffled sounds begin behind her. The confrontation had started.

At eleven-oh-five, a group of younger kids came walking down the street. They were all about twelve or thirteen years old, and several carried backpacks. Some wore festive hats or masks.

They started to turn toward the community center. Ruby said, "Hey, kids. Move along."

One of them, wearing a red party hat, turned to look at her. "Who, us?"

"Yes, you! Stay off that street. Go the other way."

"The bus stop's this way," objected the kid in the red hat.

"Don't care. You go around."

"Listen, lady," said the kid in the red hat, annoyed, "we need to get home."

"Yeah," said another kid, wearing a blue mask, "and we're already late."

"Not my problem," Ruby told them coldly. "You can't go down that street."

"Why not?" demanded another kid. This one wore the most elaborate costume of all: black pants and a gold shirt with a flowing black cape. He wore a black and gold mask and had a black beanie pulled down over his head. "Why can't we go that way?" this figure demanded.

"Because I said so," Ruby told him. "Now, you kids get out of here. Move."

"Hey!" cried the kid in the black-and-gold costume. "Hey, there's a fight down there!"

"It's gang business," said Ruby proudly. "You don't want to be involved."

"Hey!" cried the kid in the black-and-gold costume again. And he went running past Ruby and sprinting down the street.

"Hey, Juan!" shouted one of the other kids. "Juan, come back!"

Ruby wasn't sure what to do. If she abandoned her post to chase the one kid who'd gotten through, maybe all the others would follow. She didn't know what to do.

A sudden siren and distant flashing blue lights solved her dilemma. "Cops!" said one of the kids.

"Police!" screamed Ruby. She turned and ran down the block toward the community center, shouting, "Police! Police! Clear out, it's the cops!"

But then she stopped, stunned, when she saw what was happening in the parking lot.

The gang members from both sides were jumping around wildly, waving their arms, throwing their weapons away. Then they all started tearing off their gang jackets and throwing them away, yelling and cursing. They were making so much noise themselves that they never heard Ruby's warning. They didn't even hear the police sirens. And suddenly both parking lot entrances were filled with police officers, an officer had Ruby in custody, and the confrontation was over.

Ruby was so bewildered and frightened that everything became a blur. But in the middle of it all, she did see the small figure in the gold-and-black costume go running away down the street.

And she had the strangest feeling that it was all his fault.

The newspaper article ran the next morning:

GANG CONFRONTATION ENDS IN MASS ARREST

Forty-seven members of two rival gangs were arrested last night following a coordinated police response to a planned confrontation at the Riverside Community Center.

According to witnesses and the arrested individuals, the confrontation ended abruptly when participants began discarding their weapons and clothing. Multiple gang members reported that their metal objects—knives, chains, and belt buckles—became "too cold to touch" and that their leather jackets caused similar discomfort.

When jackets were collected as evidence, officers noted that the original gang insignias on each jacket had been obscured by what appeared to be burn marks forming the words "Phoenix Rising."

Marcus Webb, 19, leader of the Stonegate Crew, told reporters: "Something happened to us. Someone did this. I don't know how, but someone stopped the fight."

Darnell Price, 21, of the Ashford Vipers, made similar claims: "My knife got so cold it burned my hand. That's not normal. Whoever Phoenix is, they came after us."

Police spokesperson declined to comment on the unusual claims, stating only that the investigation is ongoing.

Captain Zara Riley tossed the paper onto her desk. "The gangs are playing games with the media."

Lawson had the newspaper open to the same article. "Both gangs made the same claim. Independently."

"So they coordinated their story. Gangs do that."

"Both gangs? Working together? On a story that makes them look foolish?"

Riley leaned back. "What's your alternative theory, Lawson?"

Lawson didn't answer directly. "Webb said 'someone stopped the fight.' Price said 'whoever Phoenix is, they came after us.'"

"Gang members making excuses. That's all this is."

"In Valleyview, the getaway driver said 'someone stopped us.' In Northfield, Wilson said 'someone burned me.' Both denied making the signatures."

Riley's expression hardened. "You're collecting coincidences and calling them evidence."

"Three incidents. Three claims of external intervention. Three identical signatures that no one admits to creating."

"Listen to yourself. You're describing something that doesn't exist. Whatever bizarre explanation you're cooking up—"

"I haven't offered an explanation."

"Good. Don't." Riley stood up. "I've seen this before. Martinez spent two years chasing shadows, convinced there was an arsonist conspiracy. He ended up on administrative leave. Don't make the same mistake."

Lawson gathered his papers. "Yes, ma'am."

Back at his desk, he spread out everything he had collected. The photograph of the orange spray paint on the van. The photograph of the burned letters on the rifle stock. The newspaper clipping with its photograph of a leather jacket, gang colors obscured by the same two words.

The mechanics' report on the van: steering fluid absent, no leak, residue consistent with extreme heat.

The forensics report on the rifle: anomalous heat distribution, burn pattern inconsistent with normal weapon operation.

The evidence log from the gang confrontation: multiple reports of metal objects becoming extremely cold, leather becoming uncomfortable to touch, all within moments of each other.

Three separate incidents. Three separate locations. Three sets of perpetrators with no connection to each other.

Each time, something physically impossible had happened. Each time, the same signature had appeared. Each time, the perpetrators claimed someone else was responsible.

The van's steering fluid had vanished as if superheated. The rifle had burned its owner's hands from a point far from the barrel. Metal objects in a parking lot had become cold enough to cause frostbite-like injuries.

Heat. Heat. Cold.

He looked at the signatures again. Spray paint. Burned wood. Burned leather.

Different methods. Same words. Same crude lettering style.

Lawson pulled out a blank sheet of paper and began making a timeline. September: warehouse robbery, steering failure, spray paint. November: Wilson rampage, rifle overheating, burned letters. December: gang confrontation, metal freezing, burned insignias.

He stared at the paper for a long time.

The evidence pointed toward a pattern. The physical phenomena defied natural explanation. The signatures were consistent across incidents.

He didn't write down what he suspected. He didn't need to. The photographs and reports spoke for themselves, arranged there on his desk, waiting for someone to see what connected them.

Lawson looked at the three images one more time—the van, the rifle, the jacket—then gathered everything into a single folder. He labeled it simply: "Phoenix."

He locked the folder in his desk drawer.

Whatever was happening in their city, he would keep watching.
